title: Rhythm Recognition
body:
## The five questions, in order

Rate? Regular? P for every QRS and QRS for every P? PR constant and normal? QRS narrow or wide? Then name it.

## Rhythm table

| Rhythm | Rate | Regularity | P waves | PR | QRS | First action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Normal sinus** | `60–100` | Regular | Upright, uniform, one per QRS | `0.12–0.20 s` | `0.06–0.10 s` | Nothing |
| **Sinus tachycardia** | `101–150` | Regular | Normal, may hide in the preceding T | Normal | Narrow | Find and treat the cause: fever, pain, hypovolemia, hypoxia, anxiety, drugs |
| **Sinus bradycardia** | under `60` | Regular | Normal | Normal | Narrow | Treat only if symptomatic: atropine `1 mg` |
| **Atrial fibrillation** | Atrial `350–600`, ventricular often `100–180` | **Irregularly irregular** | None — chaotic fibrillatory baseline | Not measurable | Narrow | Rate control and anticoagulation; unstable gets sync cardioversion `120–200 J` |
| **Atrial flutter** | Atrial about `300`, ventricular depends on the conduction ratio (`2:1` gives `150`) | Usually regular | Sawtooth flutter waves, best in `II`, `III`, `aVF` | Not measurable | Narrow | Rate control; unstable gets sync cardioversion `50–100 J` |
| **SVT (AVNRT/PSVT)** | `150–250` | Regular | Buried, retrograde, or absent | Not measurable | Narrow | Vagal maneuvers, then adenosine `6 mg` then `12 mg`; unstable gets sync `50–100 J` |
| **Junctional** | Escape `40–60`; accelerated `60–100`; tachycardia `100–180` | Regular | Absent, inverted before the QRS, or after it | Under `0.12 s` if visible | Narrow | Treat the cause; think digoxin toxicity and ischemia |
| **1st-degree AV block** | Underlying | Regular | Normal, `1:1` | Fixed, over `0.20 s` | Narrow | Observe |
| **2nd-degree type I (Wenckebach)** | Atrial regular, ventricular slower | Irregular, grouped beating | More P than QRS | Lengthens progressively, then a QRS drops | Narrow | Usually observe; atropine if symptomatic |
| **2nd-degree type II (Mobitz II)** | Atrial regular | Regular or irregular | More P than QRS | **Constant**, then a sudden dropped beat | Often wide | Prepare transcutaneous pacing — atropine usually fails and can worsen it |
| **3rd-degree (complete)** | Atrial `60–100`, ventricular `20–40` (wide escape) or `40–60` (narrow escape) | Both regular, unrelated | March through independently | No relationship | Narrow or wide | Transcutaneous pacing, prepare transvenous |
| **PVCs** | Underlying | Irregular when they land | None before the ectopic beat | None | Wide (`0.12 s` or more), bizarre, T wave opposite the QRS | Check potassium and magnesium, oxygenation, ischemia. Worry about runs, multifocal, and R-on-T |
| **VT, monomorphic** | `100–250` | Regular | Absent or dissociated | None | Wide, all beats identical | Pulse and stable: antiarrhythmic. Pulse and unstable: sync `100 J`. Pulseless: defibrillate |
| **VT, polymorphic** | `150–300` | Irregular | Absent | None | Wide, changing shape | Defibrillate (unsynchronized) if pulseless; treat ischemia |
| **Torsades de pointes** | `150–250` | Irregular | Absent | None | Wide, twisting around the baseline | Magnesium `1–2 g` IV; defibrillate if pulseless; stop QT-prolonging drugs |
| **Ventricular fibrillation** | No countable rate | Chaotic | None | None | None — pure quiver | CPR and defibrillate now |
| **Asystole** | `0` | Flat | Sometimes P waves only | None | None | CPR and epinephrine; confirm in two leads and check leads and gain |
| **PEA** | Any organized rhythm | Varies | Varies | Varies | Varies | **No pulse.** CPR, epinephrine, and hunt the H's and T's |
| **Paced** | Set rate, usually `60–80` | Regular | Spike before the P (atrial), before the QRS (ventricular), or both | N/A | Wide, LBBB-like on ventricular pacing | Confirm capture: every spike followed by a complex, and a pulse to match |

> **Trap:** A regular narrow-complex rhythm at exactly `150` is atrial flutter with `2:1` conduction until you prove otherwise. Slow the AV node and the sawtooth shows itself.

## STEMI criteria

New ST elevation at the J point in **two contiguous leads**:

| Leads | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Any lead except `V2`–`V3` | `1 mm` (`0.1 mV`) |
| `V2`–`V3`, men under `40` | `2.5 mm` |
| `V2`–`V3`, men `40` and older | `2 mm` |
| `V2`–`V3`, women, any age | `1.5 mm` |
| `V7`–`V9` (posterior) | `0.5 mm` |
| `V3R`–`V4R` (right) | `0.5 mm` (`1 mm` in men under `30`) |

Also treat as a STEMI equivalent: new left bundle branch block with a concerning clinical picture (use the Sgarbossa criteria), tall R waves with ST depression in `V1`–`V3` (posterior MI), and `aVR` elevation with diffuse ST depression (left main).

Reciprocal ST depression in the opposite wall makes the elevation far more likely to be real.

## Hyperkalemia progression

| Potassium | ECG |
|---|---|
| `5.5–6.5 mEq/L` | Tall, narrow, peaked, symmetric T waves; shortened QT |
| `6.5–7.5` | P waves flatten and disappear; PR lengthens |
| `7.0–8.0` | QRS widens; bradycardia; junctional rhythms |
| `8.0–9.0` | QRS merges with T into a sine wave |
| Above `9.0` | Ventricular fibrillation or asystole |

> **Key:** Peaked T waves in a dialysis patient are a calcium-now finding, not a wait-for-the-lab finding.

## QTc thresholds

| QTc | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Under `0.35 s` | Short QT — think hypercalcemia, digoxin |
| Up to `0.44 s` (men) / `0.46 s` (women) | Normal |
| `0.47 s` or more (men) / `0.48 s` or more (women) | Prolonged |
| `0.50 s` or more | Meaningful torsades risk — review every QT-prolonging drug |
| `0.60 s` or more | High risk |
